The Common dragonet Callionymus lyra exhibits a markedly sexually dimorphic growth pattern, a trait common among benthic-dwelling callionymids. In northern European waters, field surveys indicate that females attain an ultimate total length of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], while males can reach a considerably larger ultimate total length of 30.5 cm [Li = 30.5 cm]. This divergence in maximum body size is thought to reflect sexual selection pressures, as larger males often secure better spawning territories on sandy substrates. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), measured under local thermal conditions at 13.3 °C [T = 13.3 °C], averaged 6.5% [GSI = 6.5%]. This index was calculated from gravid females collected at a mean water temperature of 13.3 °C [T = 13.3 °C], a thermal regime typical of its North Sea habitat.

Recruitment success in Callionymus lyra hinges on the delicate transition from the pelagic larval phase to its benthic juvenile existence. When incubated at 13.3 °C [T = 13.3 °C], hatching from the egg occurs at an age of 4 days [ab = 4 days]. The newly emerged prolarvae possess a minimal wet weight at birth of only 0.000051 grams [Wwb = 0.000051 grams] under the same thermal regime. This incredibly low mass derives from the small egg diameter of roughly 0.46 mm, a trait that produces a yolk-sac larva with limited endogenous reserves. The yolk absorption stage is consequently brief, and the onset of exogenous feeding must occur quickly to avoid starvation. This 4-day incubation period at the given temperature represents a relatively fast developmental rate compared to some other temperate gobiesocids, allowing the larvae to exploit the spring plankton bloom. Following the hatching event, the free-swimming larvae then undergo a brief planktonic period before metamorphosing and settling onto the seabed.

Growth trajectories during the juvenile phase are closely tied to the transition to a benthic lifestyle. Following larval metamorphosis and settlement, the young dragonets begin a period of rapid somatic growth. The onset of sexual maturation is a key life history event, and in this species, the total length at puberty is observed to be 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm]. Corresponding to that length, the wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 2.08 grams [Wwp = 2.08 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship and consistent with the modest size at which gonadal recrudescence begins in small benthic teleosts. Reaching this size requires the successful navigation of high juvenile mortality rates, which are typical for small demersal fish. The age at which this length threshold is reached can vary considerably depending on local food availability and water temperature.

Once the gonadal tissues have fully matured, the adult size structure becomes sharply defined. Females ultimately reach a stable adult body mass of approximately 42.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 42.7 grams], a figure based on the length-weight relationship recorded for the species. Most of the reproductive population consists of fish that are still actively growing, and the life history strategy appears to emphasize early maturation at the expense of achieving a very large adult size. The energetic demands of producing two annual spawning batches likely constrain the resources available for further somatic expansion. With a maximum adult body mass of roughly 42.7 grams [Wwi = roughly 42.7 grams], Callionymus lyra is placed among the smaller members of the benthic fish community on the continental shelf, where sexual dimorphism in size is pronounced.

Natural mortality eventually curtails reproductive activity, and the maximum recorded lifespan for Callionymus lyra provides a window into its generation time. Based on analysis of length-frequency data, the maximum longevity is estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] in the wild at a mean ambient temperature of 13.3 °C [T = 13.3 °C]. This value, equivalent to approximately 2555 days, is typical for a small, iteroparous demersal fish that experiences moderate predation pressure. The species shows no evidence of a dramatic post-spawning death; instead, senescent individuals gradually decline in condition. Across its geographic range, this lifespan may vary slightly; in warmer southern waters, metabolic acceleration might shorten the maximum age, while in colder northern fjords, individuals might persist slightly longer. The 7-year maximum age allows for several successive spawning seasons in a typical individual's life, underscoring the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy.
